passage: Thursday night. Today Kabir put Hemant's bag on the roof of the cycle shed and everyone laughed. I laughed too, really loud, so nobody would think I was boring. Hemant looked straight at me for one second. Now my stomach feels weird and I couldn't finish dinner. I keep thinking I should have said something. I did not mean it, but I did laugh, and that is the thing. Tomorrow I will say sorry to Hemant first thing, before class. And if Kabir does something like that again, I won't laugh. I will walk away or stand next to Hemant. No excuses in my head this time. -- Raghav

qa.q: Where did Kabir put Hemant's bag?
qa.a: Kabir put it on the roof of the cycle shed.

qa.q: Why does Raghav feel sick tonight?
qa.a: Raghav laughed along with the others and remembers Hemant's look, so guilt is at work, and the plan to apologise shows Raghav's conscience is working.

qa.q: What does Raghav plan to do next, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Raghav plans to say sorry to Hemant first thing tomorrow and not laugh if it happens again, which turns guilt into action instead of excuses.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt when looking at Raghav during the laughing?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt hurt and let down that a friend was laughing, since Hemant looked straight at Raghav for one second.

grounding: A child who laughed along at someone feels guilt, plans an apology and to refuse next time.

passage:
In the hostel common room, the older boys were copying Harsha's accent, and everyone laughed. Lalit laughed too, loud, so no one would notice he wasn't part of the joke.
Harsha went red and walked out.
That night in his bunk, Lalit's stomach churned. He kept seeing Harsha's back going through the door. He felt sick. He almost told himself Harsha was too sensitive.
But he knew that wasn't true.
In the morning, he found Harsha at the washbasins. "I'm sorry I laughed yesterday. It was mean. I won't do it again."
Harsha looked at him. "Thanks." When the boys started again that evening, Lalit didn't laugh. He left the room.

qa.q: Where were the older boys copying Harsha's accent?
Why did Lalit's stomach churn in his bunk?
qa.a: He felt guilty and sick about laughing along, knowing he had hurt Harsha.

qa.q: What did Lalit do with his guilt that was better than defending himself?
qa.a: He apologised to Harsha the next morning and refused to join in when the teasing started again.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Lalit apologised?
qa.a: Harsha may have felt surprised and a bit relieved that someone saw it was wrong.

grounding: A boy laughs along when others mock a hostel mate, later feels sick with guilt, apologises to him and refuses to join in next time.

passage:
Monday. Seema whispered that Kunal's shirt looked like his grandfather's, and Pranav laughed along. Kunal heard. He pulled his jumper over the shirt.
Tuesday. Pranav couldn't eat his lunch. He kept picturing Kunal's hands tugging the jumper down. He felt a little sick. Part of him wanted to say, "It was only a joke," but that didn't feel honest.
Wednesday. Pranav sat next to Kunal at break. "I'm sorry I laughed about your shirt. It wasn't fair."
Kunal shrugged, but his shoulders loosened.
Later, Seema started another joke about someone's shoes. Pranav shook his head. "Not funny, Seema." He walked off to play football.

qa.q: What did Seema say about Kunal's shirt?
qa.a: That it looked like his grandfather's.

qa.q: What does Pranav not eating his lunch suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt guilty and uneasy about laughing at Kunal.

qa.q: What did Pranav choose instead of defending himself as "only a joke"?
qa.a: He apologised to Kunal and, when Seema joked again, refused to join in.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Pranav's apology?
qa.a: Kunal seems cautious but a little relieved, since his shoulders loosen even though he only shrugs.

grounding: A boy laughs along at a classmate, later feels sick with guilt, apologises to him and refuses to join the next joke.
